Can FinBERT Improve Analyst Triage?

A point-in-time study using real SEC earnings releases

Author

Shane Conway

Published

November 22, 2026

Abstract

This study asks whether a pinned financial-language model adds useful ranking information beyond a transparent word-count baseline. The feature documents are 68 real earnings-release exhibits furnished through SEC Form 8-K filings by six large issuers from 2020 through 2025. Each release is timestamped at EDGAR acceptance and paired with next-quarter year-over-year revenue growth calculated from facts that became public in a later SEC filing. The first 45 observations form development evidence; 23 releases accepted in 2024–2025 form the later test. The lexicon records a test Spearman rank information coefficient of 0.501, while pinned FinBERT records 0.624. Their paired difference is 0.122, but a 90 percent issuer-block bootstrap interval spans -0.351 to 0.553. A top-third review policy also concentrates high-growth observations, but its evidence is small, issuer-concentrated, and not a return or profit estimate. The warranted decision is therefore to retain the transparent baseline while extending the population and preserving a new later test. The project demonstrates how to join real SEC documents, model scores, future labels, uncertainty, and decision authority without converting a promising point estimate into an unsupported victory claim.

1 Research question and decision

The question is deliberately comparative and allowed to fail:

Does ProsusAI/finbert, pinned to revision 0bc2ac10dda6929bcb1f77ccc43c7ec5c424f031, rank next-quarter year-over-year revenue growth better than a transparent lexicon on a later set of real SEC earnings releases?

The proposed use is analyst triage, not trading. If an analyst can inspect only one third of new releases, the reader ranks which documents receive deeper review. The design therefore evaluates both the continuous score and a fixed top-third capacity rule. It does not claim that future revenue growth is directly tradeable or that selected documents would produce excess returns.

2 What the SEC records are

Form 8-K is a current report used for specified events under the Securities Exchange Act (U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission 2025). In the observations selected here, Item 2.02 reports results of operations and financial condition, while Item 9.01 identifies the attached exhibits. Exhibit 99.1 is the earnings release converted to plain text and scored. The 8-K filing-detail page is therefore the folder and index; the exhibit is the document the model reads.

The Apple observation used throughout the course makes the objects concrete. EDGAR accession 0000320193-23-000005 was accepted on February 2, 2023 at 16:30:33 Eastern time. Its filing-detail page lists Item 2.02 and links Exhibit 99.1 (Apple Inc. 2023b). The exhibit reports Apple’s quarter ended December 31, 2022, including quarterly revenue of $117.2 billion and the accompanying management language (Apple Inc. 2023a).

The future outcome is a different object. The downloader obtains structured XBRL revenue facts from a later SEC filing, selects the next fiscal quarter and its same-quarter prior-year comparison, and computes year-over-year growth. XBRL facts include a concept, value, unit, period, and filing provenance. They are used as later labels; they are not included in the text supplied to FinBERT.

3 Population, clocks, and provenance

The fixed teaching cohort contains Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Caterpillar, Coca-Cola, and IBM. The downloader selects original Form 8-K Item 2.02 earnings-release exhibits accepted during 2020–2025. An observation survives only if a later filing supplies a clean quarterly revenue duration fact and a same-filing prior-year comparison. Fourth-quarter values that would require annual-minus-nine-month derivations are excluded.

Every row retains the issuer CIK, 8-K accession, EDGAR acceptance time, selected exhibit filename and URL, content hash, outcome quarter, later label date, and later filing accession. These fields make the information contract inspectable.

Figure Figure 3 separates three dates that are easy to confuse. The quarter end describes the business period. The 8-K acceptance time bounds when the release text became public. The later filing date bounds when the future outcome became observable. Aligning text to quarter end would move language backward in time. Using the later revenue fact as a feature would directly reveal the label.

The cohort is small by design. Forty-five observations accepted through 2023 serve development and illustration; 23 observations accepted in 2024–2025 form the untouched later comparison. This fixed six-issuer sample improves inspectability but limits external validity.

4 Readers and frozen procedure

The transparent baseline counts a printed set of positive and negative finance terms and divides their difference by the total number of positive and negative hits. Finance-domain dictionaries are important because words can carry meanings in financial reports that differ from ordinary language (Loughran and McDonald 2011). The small baseline used here is intentionally simpler than a production Loughran–McDonald implementation; its vocabulary is visible in analysis.py.

The candidate is FinBERT, a BERT model adapted to financial sentiment classification (Araci 2019). The checkpoint is pinned by revision rather than named only by repository. Each complete release is tokenized, and at most eight evenly spaced windows of 480 tokens are scored. Class probabilities are averaged across windows, and the document score is positive probability minus negative probability. This aggregation is part of the model specification.

Neither reader was trained here to predict next-quarter revenue growth. The experiment therefore tests whether a sentiment representation supplies useful downstream ordering, not whether FinBERT is an accurate revenue model.

5 Evaluation and uncertainty

The primary metric is Spearman rank information coefficient: the correlation between the ordering induced by a reader and the ordering of later revenue growth. Rank IC is suitable for the triage question because the policy allocates scarce review capacity by rank. It is not a return measure.

Uncertainty is estimated with 2,000 paired issuer-block bootstrap resamples using seed 20261122. An issuer is the resampling unit, and all of its test observations move together. The same resampled issuers are used for both readers so the incremental difference is paired. The interval does not repair the small number of issuers; it makes that uncertainty visible without pretending that 23 rows are 23 independent companies.

6 Results

The lexicon test rank IC is 0.501, and FinBERT’s is 0.624. Those point estimates favor the richer reader. The relevant incremental estimate, however, is only 0.122, with a 90 percent paired interval from -0.351 to 0.553.

The interval includes both a substantial reversal and a large improvement. Accordingly, the result supports continued investigation, not replacement of the baseline.

The top-third policy converts the score into a visible use. All test observations average 18.3 percent next-quarter year-over-year revenue growth. The eight FinBERT-selected observations average 46.5 percent, and the lexicon-selected observations average 44.3 percent. Those means are influenced by unusually high NVIDIA growth quarters and carry wide issuer-block intervals.

The figure evaluates allocation of analyst attention. It supplies no stock return, portfolio, turnover, transaction cost, or market-capacity evidence.

7 Decision, robustness, and limitations

The current evidence supports three statements: both readers rank this small later cohort positively; a top-third review rule can be evaluated; and the candidate is worth testing on a broader population. It does not establish a stable incremental FinBERT advantage, a market-wide relationship, or a trading claim.

The operating decision is therefore conservative: keep the transparent reader, expand the issuer population, predeclare any revised text aggregation or outcome definition, and reserve a genuinely new later period for the next comparison.

The study has material limitations. Six surviving large issuers are not a market universe. Twenty-three test releases provide weak precision. The baseline is small. Revenue growth is only one downstream outcome. The bootstrap represents issuer concentration but not every source of time-series or model uncertainty. The project is historical teaching evidence rather than a preregistered study, and it does not estimate economic profits.

8 Reproducibility and the two report pathways

The root-level download_sec_data.py recreates the SEC ledger and records source URLs and SHA-256 hashes. analysis.py --score-finbert recreates model scores with the pinned checkpoint; the committed score ledger supports a lightweight offline run. summary.json contains the reported metrics, while RESEARCH_RECORD.md states the clock, split, decision, and limits.

Pathway 1 is an integrated notebook in pathway1_integrated_notebook/analysis.ipynb. Pathway 2 consists of the concise analysis notebook beside this paper. Both call the same root-level pipeline and must produce the same evidence. The separate paper may improve explanation; it may not reopen model selection after the final test is visible.

9 Conclusion

The empirical point estimate favors FinBERT, but the evidence does not establish that the richer reader improves reliably on a transparent word-count baseline. That bounded negative conclusion is the useful result. The project shows what the actual SEC data are, which document the model reads, when the feature and label become public, how uncertainty changes the sentence, and why a model’s authority should not exceed the population and decision that were tested.
